author: buchanan_robert
text: The world is full of weeping women, And of children that have never known laughter, But they are not so sad as I, who weep because my God cannot hear me speak! Who have lost all love for men, because all men are false, And am doomed to live and die alone, Because my Lord has left me here!

author: cushag
text: “The first night after they come I always lie awake.” He is an old bachelor, “always” having been for thirty years the owner of this house—an old, lonely farm house, standing on one side of a long, silent lane, at the end of which lies the village churchyard. In front rises a hill covered with thick wood. Beyond that again stretches the sea. The waves are breaking loud at times, but when all things are still the moon rising out of the water looks like a great silver fish swimming away over the ocean into the sky. But now the weather has changed

My father was an old man who fished alone
In a leaky boat, while his son played hooky
Down by the muddy slop where trout less finny
Swam upstream to die. Young men catch fish
Thick as they fall from sky. I am just now Come back from far off Tongking where at forty
Five my long johns were turning moldy brown.
But when did any son say "father," or blacken ocean floor for love?
The young do not know how wayward is Love.

Which of these poems does your heart like best?

author: buchanan_robert
text:
In this poem (a sonnet) I had forgotten what love is,
But in another way—for all my life
The truth about that thing came back at last.

It was not like this then:—but something sweet
That I never knew before, as though a lover
Had told me things I thought I did not want to know.

Then I forgot again; but now I know,
For some strange reason, since you were away from me,
How much the world is made up of the little things we see.

Perhaps a woman knows more than you

author: buchanan_robert
text:
There is music for those who listen

And love one another,

For little birds that sing on mountain tops,

author: cushag
text:
In thim days, when men were brave
And women could endure,

Thaim that didn't work would starve;
There was no dole to lure.

Then you saw children with their hands full of apples
To sell in the street or on the doorsteps ;

You never heard o’ boys selling matches—
Not then! No sirree-o !

When you saw them begging, they had nothing but bread,
Or potatoes, or peas, and some few coppers

They did not have more than sixpence,
The lowest price a father would charge

author: emily_dickinson

text:
Me Ma said it were " good-by,"

But she didn't seem to mean it;

She turned round an' spoke again—

" Now we are off to marry.

The larder's all empty!

All you lads that have come here
I'll pay for with my love.

author: cushag
text:
I had five little pigs—
John and Ma said it was too bad;
I got rid of four
By sellin' 'em all to tad.

author: cushag
text:
Come down to the mill in a shower,

Tho it rains or thunders.

I am not much afeard of thunder,

But it makes you wet as water.

author: emily_dickinson
text:
The flowers are not so sweet,
 The birds are not as gay;
 They do not sing for me,
 They sleep away the day.

author: john_keats

text:
I write it here for every child who looks
At books when old or young;
For the sweet thoughts that come from these two leaves,
I’d like them if they were brought to me on wings!

Still another poem:

The winds are blowing low to sea,
And over hill and hollow wild
Comes a wind that whistles through the trees,
With music strange and thrilling mild.

You hear it? Can you feel its power?
Can you see how softly it comes?
Do you know what joy it can impart?
Listen with ears more keenly

author: emily_dickinson
text: I know what will happen if You do not look at me; If you only leave it to chance To say good morning to thee! [Illustration: "WHAT WILL HAPPEN IF YOU DO NOT LOOK AT ME?" ]

author: emily_dickinson
text: I never saw a man who was so happy as he was that day; his face shone with joy, for his wife had borne him seven children in twelve months.

author: john_keats
text:
The day was calm; no sea-breeze blew;
But gently from the west the wind did steal;
From time to time it stirred the leaves of trees,
Which in their pride and majesty were dressed:
So slowly moved the waters deep below,
As if they waited for some great god’s decree—
Some angel down to bless the scene below,

author: john_masefield
text:
The clouds in white or silver seem
To flutter up against each room;
But when they touch its walls and beams,
They vanish like mist from a broom.

What is the meaning of this? — I have looked in vain for some explanation, except that which was given me by Mr. B., who knows better than any one else how Milton's poetry has been mutilated and perverted; but even his explanation only makes it more puzzling. He tells me that this stanza (and it does seem rather an unusual feature of Paradise Lost) was originally written thus, as follows: "The mighty engine shook not, nor could shake." Why should it, if "the wings were full of thunderbolts," and "of death" ? The first clause in each

author: john_keats
text:
He has no love for those who wish him well:
If one should kiss him on each cheek for joy;
Or if some friend might take him out to tell
The pleasantest things they ever heard of;—
'Tis vain: such is not this great lord's employ;
For none can make him think it worth their while:
His heart would shrink at every friendly smile.

author: john_keats
text: The walls are hung in many pieces with tapestries; here hang portraits of kings and queens, lords and ladies. Some are very rich tapestry and finely wrought, but some are old and decayed, worn threadbare, stained and ragged with time: you can hardly look at these without laughing at their wretched appearance. Others are large pictures or small statues of fine gold or silver, looking like precious stones. But above all there is an immense gallery richly adorned, with pillars of black marble, and the ceiling inlaid with gold leaves. This room is called “the great hall,” because it has been used for

author: john_masefield
kemp_harry_1883_1960
text: "The old man spoke again in a low voice: "We are not so far apart as you might think." And he put his hands through mine and held them close beside him. The fingers touched together, but they did not clasp. His were worn and thin, but strong, while my own had been made soft by much writing. He looked at them for a moment then said quietly: "What do I know? There is nothing more in life than this, except dying. Do you understand?" And he shook his head sadly."

"When I remember my old home town
In which my days were passed away,
My mind is full of thoughts of bygone times,
Of all the things that were so dear to me,
And especially those memories of
The quiet walks and talks I had with him.
For he seemed like a part of my own soul."

Which piece do you think has been written first?

author: john_masefield
text:
"Her eyes had been like a light in my dark room.
There never came another day that did not bring back this memory, till I saw her again."

This could well have come from two different writers who both happened upon the word "will", but it is more likely to have come out of one pen, as it so often does, when there are many pens at hand, especially where a bookkeeper and an editor were concerned. (The "mother" in each instance may also have something to do with the author being male.)

author: john_masefield
text:
"We're all at sea together now, my son,
All men are tossed upon a raging main."

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
There was no time in my life when I hadn’t
seen ships, as far back as I can remember. . ..

Then they began to be bigger and larger
and stranger—they grew so high above my head

That I wondered if they would fall down. .

I used to see them on my way home from school,
at night; the light would catch their sides and make
them glitter all over with gold and silver; or
sometimes they were painted black.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
He who would eat must plow, And he who
would live must labor, And it is good to see the sun rise on the
working man.
The man who is never happy has no business being alive.

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
— Yes, it is so; all life is like the waves,
But some are little as an insect’s wing,

While others rise in thunder-storms above

The cloud-tops, while we watch them from below.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text: How did it come to pass that I became so lean?

author: robert_frost
text: I saw some Greeks, from whom I learned that in all the world there is no more bitter toil than to plough in foreign soil. The Romans have an evil custom; they sell their own slaves for sale into other lands, and then make them do the work of men who are free.

The body’s sick; but when I look at it thus,

I see the soul in that poor frame express itself.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
He had many friends; but Philip's faith in
Christ* led him to give them up, rather than
have them share his faith, or follow Christ himself.*

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
I know the day is short, that hath been but a night;

The year, though long, will pass, and then I shall die.

author: robert_frost
text:
"There are many ways in which you may show
How much you value me; such as this for instance:-
'Here's something to feed my horse! Now go,
And let me know if he eats it all up!'—
Or thus, more plainly, 'Get your master here,
To tell me why he sent the boy away.'"

author: stephen_crane
text:
"What then, dear fellow? I see you are not happy;
Perhaps we had better part? No, no! my love is strong enough
To bear all storms; nor shall our joys be ever dimmed or darkened.
Though often vexed, yet still they come again, more bright and warm.

"They said, 'We are poor; give us work to do.
Give us something to feed on—work! Why not?'
I thought they wanted something for nothing,
And made my face look grave, as if I meant
To turn them down, or make their mouths water
With empty promises. But then I found
That only one man in two asked me this,
Which made it easier for me to refuse them,
Thinking I had more sense than all the rest.
It seems to come from habit now; you find
Many men living on charity quite

author: robert_frost
text:
"It is quite true that I don't much care for
The poor," said our old friend, "for they're all
A curse upon themselves; they'll never do
Anything in this world, except they come
To me or some other rich man. They've been
Sucking up to people ever since creation,
And all the way through history you hear them
Crying on their father's knees for something given—
Something to make life easier than it has
Been. To talk about charity as if it were
Your duty, why,

author: robert_frost
text:
The woman stands alone in the street;
She has no home or friend; she is old and lean
And bent, and her eyes are worn from want of sleep.
As if she had not met a kind face since
Her heart broke, and so much had gone amiss;
As one who asks in vain for relief or hope—
She wanders till a passing man draws near.

author: stephen_crane
text:
Two little kittens playing so well.
 When they saw an old cat coming up,
 They scampered behind her,
 Like she was a beautiful lady.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
How happy was I as a boy
 When first I learned my letters!
 How simple and how easy it seemed
 To spell such words as "boy," "day,"
 And "cat" and even "men"!
 But now I find this knowledge is but one
 Of many which I have lost;
 For in reality I am far from knowing
 What I once thought that I knew best.

The above are examples of what critics call nonsense verse, or poems written for children (though not exclusively so). The nonsense rhymes are supposed to be nonsensical, but you will notice that

"The story is true," said they,
 "And it happened long ago;
 But as you're passing by our door,
 Why not come and listen to-night?"
 The old woman came next day.
 She had never been inside.
 At last she heard all about
 The magic bird which lived outside.
 He was only three inches high--
 In stature tiny but big with wit,
 And cleverer than any one.
 The people of his country gave
 Him power over the waters,
 The fish which swam below,
 All creatures who could swim

author: stephen_crane
text:
Little Robin and Little Bobble.
I wonder how many times they have fought?
They go along together side by side.
It is true, they are both quite nice.
Their mother's name was Mabel,
She always put them to bed at five o'clock.
Then she went off to work,
And left the two brothers all alone.

author: stephen_crane
text:
Four friends in a room were talking.
 There was one who could not speak,
 And there was another deaf;
 But they never failed to talk.
 The third, being lame and blind,
 Could only nod his head yes or no.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
For all things hold an intercommunicating law,
Which we call magnetism : this binds together, and yet sets free,
The universe in every space, and time and place,

By which, each particle of matter finds a mate,
Its like and kindred, for that mutual soul, who lives within,
Whose centre holds the world, or sun, and moon, and stars, and you;

Where, everything, with all, at once, becomes one thing,
One, indivisible, perpetual act ; then only comes
This universal, eternal, uncreated thought

author: thomas_hardy
text:
In this wide world there's none so lonely; and yet
None but myself can give my heart a home.

How oft, when I have seen such sights unfold,
Or gazed at some new form that life had shown,
I've felt an impulse like a gentle wind,
To say, 'The beauty lives, and where it lies.'
But soon that impulse fled, with vague and blind
Impulses for my soul. Then would I lie down;
For then was still more power to keep me bound
From all I sought so long to find alone.
Now, though I know this vision may be vain,
My heart yet longs to feel it nearer drawn :

author: stothert_james_a
text: How many hours I have spent alone in this beautiful city! How happy was I then! What could be more charming and delightful? The vastness and extent of this place seem to me almost like a miracle. It seems impossible to describe the grandeur which you behold every where around you. In truth one never can conceive any thing greater or grander; no one who had not visited Rome would understand how magnificent it is. Here are immense buildings which will astonish you even after having seen so many other cities. Every time you look at them they appear to be quite new and different from what they were

author: stothert_james_a
text:
Here, too, if we can read his meaning's lines,
The Spirit who is Love and Life shall shine ;
And so, when Love was formed upon our earth,
Earth's first great Teacher showed her heavenly birth.

author: thomas_hardy
text:
The wind blew cold all night
 On hills of pine beside
 The river that had white
 Its shores with blossoms wide;
 But never did its chillest blow
 Make me remember I was not alone!

author: william_wordsworth
text:
I WANDERED out among the hills
 To find that I had never been;
 My heart was gay as if it still
 Had wandered many days agone.

 The sun went down behind my head,
 The air grew cold around me now;
 I took the road that leads to bed,
 Where I am going through the snow.

“I shall not be long
 With my words gone away,
 I do not fear, for though
 The wind is strong,
 It can blow nothing very far,
 For it always comes back again.
 There are things which cannot be, but they were not meant to be;
 You may not know them all, nor me either, yet you may guess
 That something might have been, had I lived on another street.”

author: thomas_hardy
thomas_hardy
text:
THE road is white, smooth, green,
 The day is warm and bright;
 What are you doing, friend?
 What have you got that I don’t?”

I am not quite sure but I hear him say,
  “What have you brought, O friend, that I want?”

author: william_wordsworth
text:
I saw thy face in the river once;
 I know not what thou wert or wherefore.
 The water glimmered on its surface,
 And at the bottom lay all white.

author: buchanan_robert
text: "I come from another world—the World-of-Shadows."

I am an Englishman, I love this land,
 This ancient country, which gave me birth;
 And if all else had perished, still were I
 Glad in my native soil: but such good-will
 To Britain has been kindled in my heart,
 That when she suffers, 'tis my sorrow too.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
When I behold this little world (if earth may have its name)
 All round the sun revolve in order fair,
 With mighty planets, with innumerable stars,
 And see how all these move in perfect laws,
 Each creature finds itself at ease or pain;
 I cannot but reflect the soul must please
 To know her Maker, when she sees him reign
 So happily over his vast domain.
 I will not doubt he has ordained us too
 To live in pleasure like them, which makes me rue
 That we are so imperfect, so unfree,
 So sadly wretched,

author: william_wordsworth
text:
Star of the East! O’er all the earth arise,
 From out whose radiance all its beauties shine;
 Whose glories gild each happy dwelling-place,
 And light the paths of ev’ry mortal race:
